title: Minimax Pointwise CATE Estimation with Unequal Nuisance Smoothness and Unknown Bounded Design Density
banked_reason: D-0.5 NO-PASS after revision cap 6: lem:control-pair-identity omitted positive-band/Hölder dependencies; mathematical kernel not refuted.
gap_reasons: The lemma assumes only iid sampling and binary support but invokes selected continuous versions of e, mu0, and tau, whose existence/uniqueness needs the density and Hölder conditions or an explicit P in P_band restriction.
proof_attempt_summary: The proposal author produced six versions of the positive-band pointwise CATE frontier, and the D-0.5 reviewer retained a field-tier assessment of its novelty. The final review still found that lem:control-pair-identity used continuous conditional versions without the positive-band and Hölder dependencies needed to justify them. The supervisor directed a terminal stop after the revision cap; the mathematical kernel was not refuted, and no D0 derivation or Lean proof was attempted.
tldr: A scalar observed-law treatment contrast may be smooth even when the propensity and control regression have unequal and individually rough Hölder orders. The theorem determines the exact pointwise mean-absolute minimax rate over every law whose unknown design density is merely measurable and bounded above and below, for unequal nuisance orders and arbitrary finite contrast order. A total close-pair local-polynomial estimator attains the frontier; the converse imports the proved exact-uniform unequal-order component certificate and requires only its explicit public-radius and lower-bound interior-slack embedding. The equal-order fixed-positive-design slice with repository density-envelope index \(\kappa_{\mathrm{repo}}=0\) is inherited; the contribution is the arbitrary-band unequal-order extension, whose rough branch depends on \(\alpha+\beta\) and cannot be obtained by substituting parameters into an equal-order theorem. Gao and Han's random-design density-ratio frontier concerns integrated function loss and a nearest-neighbor procedure, not this pointwise observational positive-band experiment. Direct substitution at the equality case yields the matched order without an additional logarithmic factor. The result is a worst-case prediction-risk benchmark for one-covariate binary-outcome CATE software, not a forest-rate or coverage theorem.
gap: Kennedy, Balakrishnan, Robins, and Wasserman (2024, Theorem 1 and Section 3.3; Remark 2; Theorem 2; Appendix B.8) identify the numerical phase on a larger design class but use support gaps in the difficult lower construction and retain a design-distribution approximation condition for attainment. Gao and Han (2020, Assumption 2 and Theorem 2 on page 3; Algorithm 2 and Theorem 5 on page 7; Theorem 6 on page 8) establish a near-minimax integrated \(L^1(g_0)\) HTE frontier for two arm-specific random designs under density-ratio geometry and a nearest-neighbor procedure, not pointwise absolute risk in the observational Bernoulli-treatment experiment. Fisher (2024, Section 3.3, Theorems 3.8 and 3.10, equation (7)) gives an unknown-design upper route under procedure-level conditions, and Kim (2026, Sections 5 and 6) imposes RKHS nuisance structure in the pointwise results. The equal-order fixed-positive-design \(\kappa_{\mathrm{repo}}=0\) slice and the exact-uniform unequal-order converse are already settled, but they do not provide the complete arbitrary-band unequal-order upper theorem.
fill: The project proves a total thresholded close-pair local-polynomial upper bound uniformly over arbitrary measurable positive-band densities for \(\alpha\ne\beta\) and arbitrary finite \(\gamma\), embeds the inherited exact-uniform converse into the separately parameterized public-radius class, and combines them into the two-branch matched rate. The unequal-order rough regime \(\alpha+\beta<\gamma/(2\gamma+1)\) depends on the unrestricted sum \(\alpha+\beta\) and is a strict class extension beyond the inherited equal-order theorem. The project-specific response-interiority restriction supplies public slack only for the finite lower-bound embedding; the upper theorem holds after dropping it. Direct equality-case substitution in the matched theorem yields the elbow without an additional logarithmic factor.
